topics.description: A radical communist movement and ruling organization in Cambodia under Pol Pot, responsible for mass atrocities including the Cambodian genocide.

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: A Dead Kennedys song is titled for a "Holiday in" this country. An empire in this country developed a martial art called "lion-pounding", or bokator. The use of "killing fields" was among the atrocities committed by Pol Pot, the head of this country's (*) Khmer Rouge regime. The massive Angkor Wat temple is located in, for 10 points, what Southeast Asian country with capital at Phnom Penh?
parts.answer: Kingdom of Cambodia [or le Royaume du Cambodge, or Prĕəh Riəciənaacak Kampuciə; accept Democratic Kampuchea or Kâmpŭchéa Prâcheathippadey; accept Srok Khmae; accept “Holiday in Cambodia”]

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: In this country, Norodom Sihanouk was overthrown by Lon Nol, who was in turn overthrown in this  country’s “Year Zero.” In this country, people who wore glasses were executed in “killing fields,” as well as  the school-turned-prison S-21. (*) Pol Pot led a regime in this country, which was called the Khmer Rouge. For 10  points, name this neighbor of Vietnam, home to Angkor Wat.
parts.answer: Cambodia [prompt on Khmer Rouge before “Rouge” is said]

topics.description: The forced removal of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children from their families by Australian authorities and their placement in institutions or non-Indigenous homes.

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: The separation of these peoples’ children from their families was detailed in the Bringing them Home Report. National Sorry Day commemorates the mistreatment of these people’s “Stolen Generations.” These peoples’ myths feature a sandstone rock formation once named for (*) Henry Ayers, Uluru. For 10 points, name these people British explorers met in the Outback, the indigenous peoples of Australia.
parts.answer: Australian Aborigines [or Aboriginals; prompt on descriptions of indigenous peoples of Australia until mentioned]

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: The treatment of these people was the subject of the “black arm band” versus “white blindfold” debate in the “history wars.” The Mabo case overturned the “terra nullius” doctrine towards these people’s land. Dot painting called papunya tula is practiced among these people who created communities called outstations and performed (*) firestick farming. The report Bringing Them Home led to Kevin Rudd’s apology to these people for the forced schooling of their children as part of the Stolen Generation. In 1985, Ayer’s Rock was returned to the Anangu tribe of these people under the name Uluru. For 10 points, name these Indigenous people of Australia.
parts.answer: ANSWER: Aboriginal Australians [or Aborigines; prompt on Australians; prompt on Indigenous Australians]

topics.description: An ancient Mesopotamian empire centered on Assur and Nineveh that dominated much of the Near East, especially during the first millennium BCE.

parts.label: L
parts.question: This ruler’s grandmother forced everyone in his empire to agree to his ascension to the throne in the Loyalty Treaty of Naqi’a-Zakutu. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this emperor, who constructed a namesake library in Nineveh.

parts.label: B
parts.question: Ashurbanipal ruled this empire from Nineveh. The Biblical Jonah was forced to visit this empire.

parts.label: C
parts.question: Prior to destroying the Elamite capital brick by brick, Ashurbanipal’s armies had besieged this city after his brother tried to revolt. This city was once ruled by Hammurabi.

parts.label: L
parts.question: The region of Mesopotamia was home to some of the first civilizations in the world. For ten points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [E] Mesopotamia was able to sustain large populations due to the ease of this practice. This practice is the cultivation of crops.

parts.label: B
parts.question: [H] This Mesopotamian civilization contained the city of Ashur and had rulers like Tigaleth-Pileser and Sennacherib. Its capital, Nineveh (NIN-ih-veh), hosted the largest library in the world at the time, built by Ashurbanipal.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [M] Mesopotamia was known as the Fertile Crescent for the rich soil that the Euphrates (yoo-FRAY-tees) and this other river provided to the region. Baghdad lies on this river.

topics.description: The Habsburg archduchess and ruler of Austria and other hereditary lands who reigned during the War of the Austrian Succession and the 18th-century Enlightenment.

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: During this century, Moll King ran an underground coffeehouse in London. A queen in this century sent Gerard van Swieten to deal with a supposed vampire outbreak. A queen in this century inherited Joseph I’s land by the Pragmatic Sanction. Fake Crimean villages were built by Grigory (*) Potemkin in this century to appease an empress who defeated Pugachev’s Rebellion. “Republics of Letters” in this century were supported by Madame Geoffrin’s Salon, which hosted Encyclopedists like Denis Diderot. For 10 points, name this century in which Maria Theresa of Austria and Catherine the Great of Russia were examples of “enlightened despots.”

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: This country surrendered Silesia to Frederick the Great’s Prussia in a conflict that ended with the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle [“eye”-lah-shah-pell] and began with the Pragmatic Sanction. The “War of [this country’s] Succession” resulted in the rule of (*) Archduchess Maria Theresa in this country that, under Frans Joseph I, merged with Hungary. For ten points, name this European country ruled by the Habsburgs from Vienna.
parts.answer: Austria (accept Osterreich ¨ ; accept Austrian Empire or Kaisertum Osterreich ¨ ; accept Austria-Hungary or Austro-Hungarian Empire after “Hungary” is read)

topics.description: The Bourbon king of France who was overthrown during the French Revolution and guillotined in 1793.

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: A ruler with this name started the War of Spanish Succession by attempting to put his grandson on the Spanish throne. That ruler of this name apocryphally proclaimed “I am the state” and was known as the Sun King. A ruler of this name was executed by (*) guillotine in 1793, shortly before his wife Marie Antoinette. The Palace at Versailles was commissioned by a ruler with, for 10 points, what regnal name, shared by eighteen kings of France.
parts.answer: Louis [accept Louis XIV or Louis XVI]

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: One ruler with this name issued the Edict of Fontainebleau, revoking the earlier Edict of Nantes and removing the rights of Protestants. That king ruled from 1643 to 1715, was known as the Sun King, and was the (*) 14th king of France with this name. The 16th French king of this name was guillotined during the French Revolution. For 10 points, what name was held by eighteen kings of France?
parts.answer: Louis [accept Louis XIV (read as “the fourteenth”) or Louis XVI (read as “the sixteenth”)]

topics.description: A political and economic union of European states established in its modern form by the 1992 Maastricht Treaty.

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: This group’s membership was significantly expanded by the addition of a group known as the "A8". This group, which was preceded by the EEC and ECSC, was established via the 1992 Maastricht Treaty. In a move nicknamed (*) "Brexit", the United Kingdom voted to leave this organization in a referendum. The Euro is the official currency of, for 10 points, what organization of European states?
parts.answer: the European Union [or the EU; accept answers in any of the other 23 official EU languages]

parts.label: L
parts.question: This leader initiated the Empty Chair Crisis after protesting the use of foreign levies in one policy initiative. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this former French president who names Paris’s international airport. During World War II, this man commanded the forces of Free France that fought against the Vichy government.

parts.label: B
parts.question: During the Empty Chair Crisis, de Gaulle protested the CAP of this multinational organization that succeeded the European Coal and Steel Community. This organization was established by the 1992 Treaty of Maastricht.

parts.label: C
parts.question: The CAP was a group of policy initiatives and laws surrounding this industry. Productivity in this industry increased after the introduction of new technology like GMOs and chemical fertilizers in the Green Revolution.

topics.description: The privately controlled Central African territory personally owned by King Leopold II of Belgium from 1885 to 1908, notorious for forced labor and atrocities during the rubber regime.
aliases: Congo Free State of Leopold II

parts.label: L
parts.question: In a “Free State” with this name, the Force Publique terrorized workers extracting rubber. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [M] Give the name of that colony personally owned by Leopold II. The colony shared this name with two modern-day nations led from Kinshasa and Brazzaville.
parts.answer: Congo [accept Congo Free State or Republic of the Congo or Democratic Republic of the Congo]

parts.label: B
parts.question: [H] Leopold II ruled this European country, whose 1830 independence movement was kicked by a performance of the opera La muette de Portici.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [E] The Force Publique cut these body parts off of workers who failed to meet rubber quotas. The workers used these body parts to hold their knives when tapping rubber trees.

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: The kingdoms of Kuba and Luba flourished in a modern-day country with this name during the 17th century. A kingdom with this name was ruled by Afonso I, who sought to convert it to Catholicism and denounced Portuguese involvement in his realm’s slave trade. In a colony with this name, the Force Publique cut off the (*) hands of native laborers who did not meet their rubber quotas. A modern-day country with this name was seized by King Leopold II of Belgium in the 19th-century Scramble for Africa. For 10 points, give this name shared by a “Republic” and a “Democratic Republic” in Central Africa.
parts.answer: Congo [accept Democratic Republic of the Congo or Republic of Congo or Kingdom of Kongo or Congo Free State or Belgian Congo]

topics.description: The Zulu people are a major Bantu ethnic group of southern Africa whose historical kingdom became a major power in nineteenth-century South Africa.

parts.label: L
parts.question: The last king of this ethnic group, Cetshwayo kaMpande (thet-shwah-yo kaam-paan-day), was defeated by a colonial army. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [10] Name this ethnic group, which today is the largest in South Africa. A province of South Africa is named for this ethnic group and Natal.

parts.label: B
parts.question: [10] This early 19th century Zulu monarch developed the "bull horn" formation and a shorter style of spear as part of his massive military reformation. The expansion of his realm is argued to have triggered the Mfecane (m-fay-thaa-nay), a long period of social upheaval in southern Africa.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [10] The Zulu Kingdom was eventually defeated by this colonial power, whose armies were also involved in the Boer Wars in South Africa. This country's colonial possessions also included Nigeria, Canada, and Australia.
parts.answer: the British Empire [or the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, or the UK, or Great Britain]

topics.description: The Agiad king of Sparta who led the Greek defense at the Battle of Thermopylae against Xerxes I in 480 BCE.

parts.label: L
parts.question: This city’s kings were forced to eat “black broth,” a dish cooked in pork blood. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [M] Name this ancient city known for throwing Persian ambassadors into wells and being generally unhelpful during Carneian festivals. 300, or more, of this city’s troops made up most of the defenders at Thermopylae.
parts.answer: ANSWER: Sparta [or Lacedaemon; or Nea Sparti]

parts.label: B
parts.question: [E] The Spartans defeated Athens in this war, named for a peninsula in Greece. Pericles ruled during this war, as chronicled by Thucydides.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [H] This Agiad king succeeded to the Spartan throne after Cleomenes I went mad and died mysteriously. This king led Spartan troops at the Battle of Thermopylae.

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: All-girl choruses in this city inspired Alcman to codify the lyric genre of “maiden songs.” This city did not participate in one battle due to the Carneia Festival. Compulsory women’s education was established by this city’s ruler Cleomenes. Women were banned from wearing gold in this city where the agoge program trained men. The Kaidas was a cliff that this city’s residents allegedly (*) threw unhealthy babies off of. This city’s queen Gorgo was married to a king who died fighting Xerxes the Great’s Immortals at Thermopylae named Leonidas. For 10 points, name this Pelopenessian, militaristic city-state that rivaled Athens.

topics.description: A major ancient Maya city and archaeological site on Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula, known especially for the Temple of Kukulcán and the Great Ball Court.

parts.label: L
parts.question: The general Siyaj K’ak’ overthrew the king of this city in 378 CE and replaced him with a ruler from Teotihuacan. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [H] Name this Mayan city in modern-day Guatemala that was home to the Lost World complex. This city fought a series of wars with the rival city of Calakmul.

parts.label: B
parts.question: [E] Tikal’s Lost World Complex was centered on one of these structures. Teotihuacan was home to two of these structures named for the Sun and Moon, and the ancient Egyptians built a “Great” one of these structures at Giza.

parts.label: C
parts.question: [M] The Mayans also constructed a pyramid named El Castillo, or the Temple of Kukulcán, in this city. This city in the Yucatán peninsula also contained the Great Ball Court.
